arXiv:2509.04731v1 [cs.AI] 05 Sep 2025

Language-Driven Hierarchical Task Structures as Explicit World Models for Multi-Agent Learning

Brennen Hill Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Wisconsin-Madison Affiliation: Madison, WI 53706 Email: bahill4@wisc.edu
Abstract

The convergence of Language models, Agent models, and World models represents a critical frontier for artificial intelligence. While recent progress has focused on scaling Language and Agent models, the development of sophisticated, explicit World Models remains a key bottleneck, particularly for complex, long-horizon multi-agent tasks. In domains such as robotic soccer, agents trained via standard reinforcement learning in high-fidelity but structurally-flat simulators often fail due to intractable exploration spaces and sparse rewards. This position paper argues that the next frontier in developing capable agents lies in creating environments that possess an explicit, hierarchical World Model. We contend that this is best achieved through hierarchical scaffolding, where complex goals are decomposed into structured, manageable subgoals. Drawing evidence from a systematic review of 2024 research in multi-agent soccer, we identify a clear and decisive trend towards integrating symbolic and hierarchical methods with multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). These approaches implicitly or explicitly construct a task-based world model to guide agent learning. We then propose a paradigm shift: leveraging Large Language Models to dynamically generate this hierarchical scaffold, effectively using language to structure the World Model on the fly. This language-driven world model provides an intrinsic curriculum, dense and meaningful learning signals, and a framework for compositional learning, enabling Agent Models to acquire sophisticated, strategic behaviors with far greater sample efficiency. By building environments with explicit, language-configurable task layers, we can bridge the gap between low-level reactive behaviors and high-level strategic team play, creating a powerful and generalizable framework for training the next generation of intelligent agents.

1 Introduction: the triad of language, agents, and world models

The remarkable progress in artificial intelligence over the past decade has been propelled by a paradigm of scale. In the realm of Language Models (L), scaling parameters and data has led to the emergence of unprecedented capabilities in reasoning and generation (Brown et al., 2020). In parallel, for Agent Models (A), the focus has been on scaling interaction, exposing agents to vast quantities of experience within simulated environments to learn complex behaviors. Yet, as we strive to build agents that can think, plan, simulate, act, and explain themselves in dynamic, partially observed worlds, a crucial third pillar comes into focus: the World Model (W). The tight integration of these three components is the critical new frontier.

This paper addresses a fundamental question at this intersection: How can we build more general and capable agents with better world models, rather than relying on LLMs alone? We argue that for a large class of challenging problems, particularly those involving multi-agent coordination over long horizons, the implicit world models learned by end-to-end agents or possessed by LLMs are insufficient. The primary bottleneck is not the fidelity of the world simulation, but its lack of explicit, task-relevant structure.

Consider the domain of robotic soccer, a canonical microcosm for the challenges of real-world multi-agent coordination (Sammut, 2010). It features continuous state and action spaces, partial observability, non-stationarity from opponent actions, and the need for sophisticated, temporally-extended team strategies. In such a domain, the brute-force scaling of interaction data through end-to-end multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is profoundly inefficient. The core issue is not merely reward sparsity, but what we term task sparsity: the chain of coordinated actions needed to execute a meaningful strategy (e.g., a give-and-go play) is so long and specific that it is virtually impossible to discover through undirected exploration. The agent is not just looking for a needle in a haystack; it is looking for a specific sequence of needles that must be threaded in the correct order.

This position paper argues for a paradigm shift in how we conceive of and engineer World Models. We posit that the next leap in agent capabilities will come not from scaling the raw size or physical fidelity of our environments, but from scaling their structural complexity. We advocate for the design of environments that embody an explicit, hierarchical World Model in the form of task scaffolding. This involves decomposing high-level, sparse-reward objectives into a rich hierarchy of sub-tasks and subgoals, creating an intrinsic, structured learning landscape that guides agents towards complex behaviors.

To substantiate this position, we first conduct a focused, systematic review of the 2024 literature on multi-agent robotic soccer. Our analysis reveals a compelling and convergent trend: the most successful and innovative recent approaches are moving away from purely monolithic MARL and towards hybrid models that integrate symbolic planners, hierarchical policy structures, and explicit curricula. We argue that these are not disparate algorithmic improvements, but rather different manifestations of the same underlying principle: injecting task structure into the learning process to create a more effective World Model.

Building on this evidence, we propose a concrete and powerful mechanism for realizing this vision: using Large Language Models as dynamic, zero-shot environment structurers. We envision a system where an LLM (L) interprets a high-level goal and generates a hierarchical task plan. This plan is then used to configure the simulation environment, instantiating an explicit, structured World Model (W). The Agent Models (A) then learn within this scaffolded world, benefiting from the compositional structure, dense subgoal rewards, and emergent curriculum. This approach directly integrates the L, A, and W pillars, creating a synergistic loop where language provides the semantic and strategic framework that makes the world learnable for agents.

2 Related work and foundations

Our position builds upon and seeks to synthesize three critical areas of AI research: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL), which provides the architectural inspiration for multi-level policies; Curriculum Learning, which provides the pedagogical framework for structured learning; and the burgeoning field of LLM-powered agents, which demonstrates the potential of language to guide action.

2.1 Hierarchical reinforcement learning: structuring the agent

Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) directly confronts the challenges of long-horizon planning and sparse rewards by imposing a hierarchical structure onto the agent’s policy, rather than the environment. The seminal options framework (Sutton et al., 1999) formalized the concept of temporally extended actions, or options. In this framework, a high-level meta-policy learns to select from a set of options, where each option is itself a policy (a sub-policy) trained to achieve a specific subgoal (e.g., "go to the ball"). Once an option is selected, it runs until its termination condition is met, allowing the agent to reason at a higher level of temporal abstraction. This abstraction makes credit assignment over long time scales more tractable and can significantly improve exploration by allowing the agent to commit to meaningful courses of action.

However, a principal challenge in HRL has always been the discovery of useful options. Where do these sub-goals and sub-policies come from? Often, they must be hand-designed, which limits scalability, or discovered automatically, which is a notoriously difficult unsupervised learning problem. Our proposal inverts this paradigm: instead of asking the agent to discover the hierarchy internally, we propose embedding the hierarchy explicitly into the World Model. The environment itself would expose the subgoals and task structure, providing a clear and direct learning signal for the agent’s hierarchical policy layers.

2.2 Curriculum learning: structuring the learning process

The concept of curriculum learning is motivated by the intuitive observation that learning is more effective when tasks are presented in a meaningful order of increasing difficulty (Bengio et al., 2009). In the context of MARL, curricula are a common and effective technique for overcoming exploration challenges. For instance, agents might first be trained on a simplified version of the task (e.g., 1 vs. 1 soccer) before graduating to the full, complex scenario (e.g., 5 vs. 5). This structured progression helps the agent acquire foundational skills before attempting to compose them.

Many of the successful MARL approaches in robotic soccer explicitly rely on manually designed, multi-stage curricula to achieve good performance (Baghi, 2024; Li et al., 2024b). While effective, this manual design process is brittle, time-consuming, and requires significant domain expertise. It does not scale to new tasks or domains easily. A hierarchically scaffolded World Model, as we propose, offers a powerful alternative. The compositional nature of the task hierarchy, where simpler sub-tasks are prerequisites for more complex ones, creates an intrinsic curriculum. The learning progression emerges naturally from the structure of the world itself, automating the curriculum design process and making it adaptable to new, complex tasks.

2.3 Language models as agent planners and world simulators

Recent breakthroughs have demonstrated the remarkable potential of LLMs to serve as the reasoning and planning backbone for autonomous agents. Works like SayCan (Ahn et al., 2022) have shown that LLMs can decompose high-level natural language commands ("bring me a snack from the kitchen") into a sequence of executable low-level actions, crucially grounding these plans in the robot’s physical affordances, a simple but effective form of World Model. This grounds the LLM’s abstract world knowledge in the agent’s immediate physical reality.

Extending this, Voyager (Wang et al., 2023) showcased an LLM-based agent in the open-ended world of Minecraft. Voyager uses the LLM not only to plan but also to propose its own curriculum for exploration and skill acquisition, demonstrating a self-directed learning loop. These systems represent a nascent form of the L-A-W triad, where the LLM (L) acts as the reasoning core for the Agent (A) by interacting with a World Model (W) represented by game APIs or robotic affordances.

Our proposal takes this one step further. Instead of the LLM only dictating the agent’s actions, we propose that the LLM should also dictate the structure of the world in which the agent learns. This moves the LLM from being solely a component of the agent to being a co-designer of the learning environment itself, creating a much tighter and more powerful integration between the Language and World models. This also provides a potential solution to the classic symbol grounding problem (Harnad, 1990), by creating an environment where symbolic labels (subgoals generated by the LLM) are explicitly and functionally tied to specific states and behaviors within the sub-symbolic simulation.

3 From implicit physics to explicit task structures: reframing the world model

To build more capable agents, we must first be precise about what a world model is and what we require of it. In the context of reinforcement learning, any environment or simulator is, by definition, a world model. It provides the state transition dynamics (P⁡(s′|s,a)P(s^{\prime}|s,a)) and reward function (R⁡(s,a)R(s,a)) that define the agent’s reality. However, we argue that a critical distinction must be made between implicit and explicit world models.

3.1 The limitations of implicit, low-level world models

Most current agent benchmarks, from Atari and MuJoCo to sophisticated simulators like Google Research Football (Kurach et al., 2020), provide what we term an implicit, low-level World Model.

  • •

    It is a World Model because it perfectly simulates the consequences of actions according to the rules of the domain.

  • •

    It is low-level because it operates at the level of raw physics or simple game rules. The state is represented by positions, velocities, and pixel values. The model answers the question "what happens next physically?" but not "what happens next strategically?".

  • •

    It is implicit because the task structure is not an explicit part of the model. The objective, score a goal, is defined only by a sparse reward signal upon reaching a rare terminal state. All intermediate strategic concepts, such as passing, defending, or creating space, exist only implicitly and must be discovered from scratch by the agent.

This type of world model places the entire burden of abstraction, planning, and strategy discovery on the Agent Model. For complex, long-horizon tasks, this burden is simply too great, leading to the task sparsity problem and intractable sample complexity. Brute-force scaling of interaction within these flat worlds is a fundamentally inefficient path to complex behavior.

3.2 The case for explicit, hierarchical world models

We advocate for a shift towards explicit, hierarchical World Models. This type of model augments the low-level physical simulation with an explicit, symbolic, and compositional representation of the task itself.

  • •

    It is explicit because the concepts of tasks, sub-tasks, goals, and subgoals are first-class citizens of the environment API. The environment doesn’t just know the rules of physics; it knows the rules of the strategy.

  • •

    It is hierarchical because it represents complex tasks as compositions of simpler sub-tasks. The goal of executing a passing play is explicitly defined in the World Model as a sequence or graph of subgoals like player A gets ball, player B moves to open space, and player A passes to player B.

This explicit structure transforms the learning problem. The World Model is no longer a passive sandbox but an active teacher. It provides the semantic concepts (the names of sub-tasks) and the structural relationships (how sub-tasks compose) that are necessary for efficient learning and planning. The agent’s task shifts from discovering these concepts from a sea of undifferentiated experience to learning how to execute and sequence them effectively.

We can build more generalizable, explicit world models on top of LLMs. The hierarchical task structure is the explicit world model, and as we will argue, LLMs are uniquely suited to generate this structure from high-level linguistic descriptions.

4 A systematic review: the convergent trend towards structure in multi-agent soccer

To ground our position in empirical evidence, we conducted a systematic review of academic papers published in 2024 that address multi-agent robotic soccer. Our search criteria targeted work in reputable venues that focused on soccer as the primary research domain, excluding papers that merely used it as one of many benchmarks. We further filtered for work on high-level strategic decision-making rather than low-level motor control, and prioritized approaches that did not rely on massive, inaccessible computational resources. This curated survey reveals a clear, undeniable trend: a spontaneous and convergent evolution away from monolithic MARL and towards architectures that embed hierarchical and symbolic structure. These approaches, we argue, are all implicitly building a more structured World Model to make the learning problem tractable.

A summary of the most relevant papers is presented in Table 1, interpreted through the L-A-W framework.

4.1 Explicit task decomposition with symbolic planners

The most direct and powerful evidence for our thesis comes from the work of Mu et al. (2024) on the HS-MARL framework. This work is a quintessential example of building an explicit world model for agents. Instead of hoping a deep RL algorithm will discover strategy, they integrate a classical Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planner directly into the MARL loop.

The HTN planner operates on a symbolic representation of the world state and a domain description file (written in HDDL) that encodes the knowledge of how to decompose high-level tasks. For example, the goal ScoreGoal is decomposed into a logical sequence of sub-tasks like AcquireBall, MoveToShootingPosition, and ExecuteShot. This symbolic plan is, in effect, a dynamic, explicit, and hierarchical World Model for the task at hand. It represents not the physics of the world, but the logic of success in that world.

A meta-controller then uses this plan to guide the low-level MARL agents by assigning them symbolic options, policies trained to achieve specific subgoals from the plan. This architecture brilliantly solves the task sparsity problem. The RL component is relieved of the burden of discovering the entire multi-step strategy; its job is simplified to learning the execution of the sub-tasks provided by the structured World Model. This work is a direct precursor to our proposal, with the key limitation being the static, manually-authored HDDL file. Our contribution is to replace this rigid symbolic planner with a flexible, generative Language Model.

4.2 Implicit structure through curricula and reward shaping

Other successful approaches achieve a similar effect through more implicit means. The MARLadona framework (Li et al., 2024b) and the modified TiZero investigated by Baghi (2024) both rely heavily on curricula and carefully shaped reward functions. For instance, agents are rewarded for moving towards the ball, passing to teammates, or moving towards the opponent’s goal.

While framed as algorithmic improvements to MARL, these techniques can be re-interpreted as manually engineering a more structured World Model. The dense rewards for intermediate behaviors are a way of making subgoals explicit. The curriculum, which moves from 1v1 to more complex scenarios, is a way of manually controlling the complexity of the World Model to guide learning. These methods work, but they demonstrate the high cost and brittleness of manual scaffolding. Every new desired behavior requires careful, manual re-engineering of the reward function or curriculum, a task that is both an art and a science.

4.3 Structuring the agent to mirror the world

A third category of methods focuses on structuring the agent’s architecture itself, often in a way that implicitly assumes a hierarchical world. The Bayesian Strategy Networks (BSN) approach (Yang and Parasuraman, 2024) explicitly aims to decompose a complex, monolithic policy into a collection of simpler, coordinated sub-policies. This architectural choice is a strong prior that assumes the underlying problem, the World Model, is itself decomposable. By building a hierarchical agent, they are betting that it will be a better fit for a world that is inherently hierarchical. This highlights the deep connection between agent architectures and world model structure. Providing an explicitly hierarchical world would make learning such decomposed policies far more direct and efficient.

This systematic review demonstrates that the research frontier is already, organically, moving towards our proposed direction. Researchers are independently discovering that injecting structure, hierarchy, and explicit subgoals is the key to unlocking complex multi-agent behavior. Our contribution is to recognize this convergent trend, give it a name, hierarchical scaffolding, and propose a general, scalable mechanism for achieving it: the use of Large Language Models.

5 The LAW triad in action: language-driven world model scaffolding

We now formalize our central proposal: a new paradigm for agent training centered on language-driven, hierarchical world models. This framework creates a tight, synergistic loop between Language (L), Agent (A), and World (W) models.

  1. 1.

    Goal Specification (Language): A user or supervising system specifies a high-level, strategic goal in natural language, e.g., "Execute a 2-on-1 fast break on the left side, culminating in a shot from player B."

  2. 2.

    Dynamic Scaffolding (L →\rightarrow W): A Large Language Model (L) receives this instruction. Using its vast pre-trained knowledge of strategy and common sense, it decomposes the goal into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of symbolic subgoals. For the example above, the LLM might generate: "Task: FastBreakLeft; Subtasks: [(1: PlayerA_GetBall), (2: PlayerB_RunWing), (3: PlayerA_DribbleMid, depends_on: 1), (4: PlayerA_PassToB, depends_on: [2, 3]), (5: PlayerB_Shoot, depends_on: 4)]".

  3. 3.

    World Model Instantiation (World): This symbolic task graph is passed to the simulation environment’s API. The environment uses this structure to become an explicit, structured World Model (W). It now understands the active subgoals, their dependencies, and their success conditions.

  4. 4.

    Structured Learning (W →\rightarrow A): The Agent Models (A), which may have a hierarchical policy structure, begin training in this scaffolded world. The environment provides dense, intrinsic rewards whenever an agent or group of agents successfully completes a subgoal in the graph. The agents learn not only low-level execution but also how to transition between states in the high-level task graph.

5.1 Key features of a scaffolded environment

To enable this vision, the next generation of agent simulation environments must be built with a new set of core features that go beyond physics simulation.

  1. 1.

    A Hierarchical Task API: The environment must expose an API for programmatically defining tasks, sub-tasks, their dependencies, and their success conditions. This API would accept a structured format (e.g., JSON or PDDL-like descriptions) generated by the LLM, allowing for the dynamic configuration of the episode’s goal structure.

  2. 2.

    Layered and Symbolic Action Spaces: To complement hierarchical tasks, agents need hierarchical action spaces. The environment should support both low-level continuous actions (e.g., set_velocity) and high-level, symbolic, and temporally extended actions (e.g., execute_option(pass_to_teammate_3)). This allows HRL agents to interface with the world at the appropriate level of abstraction.

  3. 3.

    Intrinsic Rewards for Subgoals: The environment itself becomes responsible for reward generation based on the active task scaffold. When the success condition for (PlayerA_PassToB) is met, the environment automatically issues a positive reward to Player A and/or Player B. This makes reward shaping principled, automatic, and perfectly aligned with the task structure, removing the need for manual tuning.

  4. 4.

    Procedural Curriculum Generation: The LLM can be prompted to generate task graphs of varying complexity, creating a sophisticated, automated curriculum. It can start with single-subgoal tasks ("learn to dribble to a cone") and progressively generate more complex, multi-agent plans as the agents demonstrate mastery. It can also introduce variations and novel compositions of learned skills, directly testing for generalization.

5.2 The role of the language model: planner, curriculum designer, and explainer

In this framework, the LLM takes on three critical roles that extend far beyond simply acting as an agent’s brain:

  • •

    Zero-Shot Planner: The LLM leverages its pre-trained knowledge to act as a powerful zero-shot or few-shot planner. It can generate plausible strategic plans for a vast range of situations without needing domain-specific training, overcoming the primary bottleneck of classical planners which require hand-authored domain files.

  • •

    Curriculum Designer: By adjusting the complexity, length, and composition of the generated task graphs, the LLM becomes an automated curriculum designer, guiding the agents along a smooth and efficient learning path.

  • •

    Explainer: The symbolic task graph generated by the LLM is inherently interpretable. It serves as a natural language explanation of the agents’ strategy. This directly addresses the goal of building agents that can explain themselves. We can query the system "What is the team trying to do?" and the answer is simply the current active branch of the task graph.

5.3 Generalizing the scaffolding principle beyond soccer

The power of this language-driven scaffolding approach lies in its generality. The same architecture can be applied to any domain where success depends on long-horizon, compositional tasks.

  • •

    Collaborative Software Development: A high-level goal like "refactor the database module to improve query speed" can be decomposed by an LLM into a scaffold of sub-tasks: [write migration scripts], [add indexing to key tables], [deprecate old API endpoints], [write new unit tests]. Agent models (coding agents) would be rewarded for each successfully passed test, guiding them through the complex, multi-step process.

  • •

    Automated Scientific Discovery: An instruction like "find a chemical compound that inhibits protein X" could be scaffolded into a research plan: [literature review of similar proteins], [virtual screening of candidate molecules], [run molecular dynamics simulation on top 5 candidates], [analyze binding affinity]. An agent operating within a simulated lab environment could be guided through this scientific workflow.

In all these cases, the language-driven World Model provides the crucial structure that makes an otherwise intractable exploration problem solvable.

6 Evaluation and benchmarking in scaffolded worlds

The shift towards scaffolded environments necessitates a corresponding shift in our evaluation methodologies. Simple metrics like win rate or final task success are no longer sufficient, as they do not capture the benefits of compositional learning or sample efficiency. We propose a suite of new benchmarks and metrics specifically designed for this paradigm.

6.1 New metrics for a new paradigm

  1. 1.

    Compositional Generalization Score (CGS): This metric would measure an agent’s ability to perform a novel, complex task that is a new composition of sub-tasks it has already mastered individually. For example, if an agent has learned to pass to teammate A and dribble around an obstacle in isolation, the CGS would measure its zero-shot or few-shot performance on the combined task of dribble around an obstacle, then pass to teammate A. A high CGS would indicate that the agent is not merely memorizing policies but learning reusable, compositional skills.

  2. 2.

    Curriculum Efficiency Gain (CEG): This metric quantifies the sample efficiency improvement gained from using a scaffolded environment. It would be calculated as the ratio of samples (or wall-clock time) required for a baseline agent in a flat environment to reach a target performance level, divided by the samples required for an agent in the scaffolded environment. C​E​G=Tb​a​s​e​l​i​n​e/Ts​c​a​f​f​o​l​d​e​dCEG=T_{baseline}/T_{scaffolded}. This directly measures the value proposition of the structured World Model.

  3. 3.

    Scaffolding Brittleness Index (SBI): No scaffold, especially one generated by an LLM, will be perfect. This metric assesses an agent’s robustness to imperfect or sub-optimal scaffolding. It could be measured by injecting noise or errors into the task graph (e.g., omitting a necessary step or reversing the order of two steps) and measuring the performance degradation compared to the optimal scaffold. A low SBI indicates a robust agent that can learn effectively even with imperfect guidance.

6.2 A call for new benchmarks

To facilitate research in this area, we call for the development of new benchmark environments, such as a Scaffold-Gym, that implement the principles outlined above. Such an environment would feature a built-in API for dynamically ingesting hierarchical task graphs, managing intrinsic rewards for subgoals, and supporting layered action spaces. This would provide a standardized platform for the community to develop and compare different methods for language-driven scaffolding, hierarchical agent architectures, and compositional learning.

7 Challenges and future directions

The paradigm of language-driven scaffolding, while powerful, is not without its challenges. These challenges themselves represent fertile ground for future research at the intersection of L, A, and W.

7.1 The scaffolding design problem

While LLMs can act as powerful zero-shot planners, their output can be inconsistent, logically flawed, or ungrounded in the reality of the environment. A primary research challenge is ensuring the quality and feasibility of the generated scaffolds. This may involve a critic model that validates the LLM’s plan against the known affordances of the world, creating a feedback loop for plan refinement. Another direction is to allow agents to learn the task hierarchy itself, perhaps by using the LLM’s plan as a strong prior which the agent can then modify based on its own experience.

7.2 The trade-off: guidance vs. open-ended discovery

A significant risk of providing explicit structure is that it may over-constrain the agent’s learning, preventing the discovery of novel, out-of-the-box strategies that were not envisioned by the human prompter or the LLM planner. A rigid scaffold might lead to locally optimal but globally sub-optimal solutions. Future work must explore ways to balance guidance with freedom. This could involve scaffolding relaxation, where the environment starts with a rigid task structure and gradually makes it more flexible as the agent gains competence. It could also involve stochastic scaffolding, where the LLM proposes multiple valid plans, encouraging the agent to explore different strategic pathways.

7.3 The enduring symbol grounding problem

The effective use of a symbolic task graph depends entirely on the ability to connect its nodes to the sub-symbolic, continuous reality of the environment (Harnad, 1990). How does an agent translate the symbolic subgoal (MoveToShootingPosition) into a concrete target (x,y)(x,y) coordinate when that position is dynamic and depends on the locations of teammates and opponents? This requires powerful grounding models, likely involving multi-modal perception and attention mechanisms, that can map between the symbolic instructions of the World Model and the sensory data of the Agent Model. Developing these grounding mechanisms is perhaps the most critical technical challenge in this domain and a central focus for future L-A-W research.

8 Conclusion

The quest for more general and capable artificial agents has brought us to a pivotal moment, the integration of Language, Agent, and World models. This paper has argued that the current focus on scaling model size and interaction data, while fruitful, is hitting a wall of inefficiency in the face of complex, long-horizon, multi-agent tasks. The critical missing piece is a World Model that is not just a high-fidelity physics sandbox, but an active, structured learning environment.

Through a systematic review of the recent multi-agent soccer literature, we have demonstrated a clear, convergent trend towards embedding hierarchy and symbolic structure into the learning process. These approaches succeed because they implicitly build a more tractable, task-centric World Model for their agents. Building on this insight, we have proposed a paradigm for making this structure explicit, dynamic, and scalable: language-driven hierarchical scaffolding. By leveraging Large Language Models to interpret high-level goals and configure the environment with a compositional task structure, we create a powerful synergistic loop. The Language Model provides the strategic plan, which becomes the explicit World Model. This structured World Model, in turn, provides the ideal conditions, an intrinsic curriculum, dense rewards, and compositional building blocks, for the Agent Models to learn sophisticated behaviors efficiently.

This position is a call to action for the community of researchers and environment builders. We must shift our focus from creating worlds that are merely complex to creating worlds that are structured for learning. The development of benchmarks and platforms that treat hierarchical task definition as a first-class feature is a critical next step. By scaffolding the world, we provide our agents with the foundation they need to build the towering capabilities we envision, to not only act, but to truly plan, strategize, cooperate, and ultimately, explain their reasoning in our complex world.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
